name: Blue-light glasses

lead: Blue-light glasses filter some short-wavelength light from screens and LEDs. They come in clear lenses and fashion frames, and are sold for eye strain and sleep; appearance forums wear them hoping for brighter, less tired-looking eyes.

Tints or coatings reduce transmission of blue light, which is thought to affect comfort and the body clock. Reviews report little support for eye-strain relief, and studies exist in sleep disorders and Parkinson disease. The brighter-eyes claim has not been tested.

paras: People wear them during screen use or in the evening, and many choose them as frames for a styled look. Some wear them in the hours before bed.
Minimal risks are described. Tinted lenses can alter colour perception.

angle.text: Wearers hope that filtering screen light means less strain and better sleep, and so brighter, less tired-looking eyes, while the frames add to the styled look. Reviews of eye strain relief report little support, and the brighter-eyes effect has not been studied.

lead: Blue-light glasses, also called blue-blocking or blue-filtering glasses, are spectacles with lenses that filter part of the blue end of the visible spectrum emitted by screens and LED lighting. They are sold over the counter, often with clear or lightly tinted lenses in everyday frames, and are marketed for digital eye strain and for sleep. Amber and orange lenses filter much more blue light than clear ones and are the type used in most sleep research.[1][2][3][4]

People use them to look better in two ways. Some wear them during long screen sessions hoping for less eye tiredness and a fresher, less strained look; others put them on in the evening to protect melatonin and sleep, which feeds into how rested the face looks and how well recovery from training goes. Experimental studies of sleep restriction have reported that people who slept less were rated as looking less healthy and less attractive, which is the link users have in mind.[2][5] As eyewear they also double as a style accessory.

Research differs by use. The American Academy of Ophthalmology and the UK College of Optometrists do not recommend blue-blocking lenses for computer use or eye strain, and the AAO attributes screen discomfort mainly to reduced blinking.[6][4] For sleep, small randomized trials of amber-lens glasses have measured outcomes in athletes, pregnant women and patients with mania, with varied results, and trials of blue-light-emitting glasses have studied delayed sleep-wake phase disorder and Parkinson disease, a different, light-delivering use.[7][8][9][10][11][12] No study has tested them for making the eyes look brighter.

paras: Blue-light glasses use tints, pigments or coatings to reduce the transmission of short-wavelength light, roughly 400 to 500 nm. Grokipedia places the reduction at about 10 to 25 percent for common clear consumer lenses, with amber lenses filtering considerably more. Manufacturers' claims about the share of blue light filtered are statements by the companies, not independent measurements.[2] A 2022 spectrophotometric study in Chronobiology International compared commercially available blue blockers under multiple lighting conditions and found that products differ in what they transmit.[3]

Some products add anti-glare coatings or prescription correction. Wikipedia notes that some also block ultraviolet light, although computer monitors emit no measurable UV.[4] Glasses that emit blue light, used as a morning light therapy device, are a separate product type from lenses that block it.[10][12]

Wikipedia reports that blue-blocking glasses became increasingly popular toward the end of the 2010s in response to concern about overexposure to blue light from computers, phones and tablets.[4] Grokipedia traces precursors to early twentieth-century glare and ultraviolet protection, including cerium-glass lenses attributed to William Crookes in 1913 and aviator lenses developed by Bausch & Lomb in the 1930s, and cites a 1989 patent (US 4,878,748) for a lens that blocked ultraviolet and blue light; that AI-generated history is unverified.[2] Computer vision syndrome gained attention in the 1990s with personal computers, and consumer blue-light eyewear grew in the 2010s as LED screens and smartphone use rose; Grokipedia cites a 2014 Vision Council report that nearly 70 percent of US adults experienced digital eye strain symptoms.[1][2]

The sleep rationale is that light stimulates intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, which suppress melatonin release by the pineal gland, so blocking blue wavelengths in the evening is expected to reduce that suppression. A 2019 review describes the retina-to-pineal pathway and the influence of light exposure on melatonin.[13] The AAO states that blue light affects the body's circadian rhythm and that bright screens late at night can make it harder to fall asleep; it recommends limiting screen time for two to three hours before bed and using a device's night settings.[6]

The eye-strain rationale is less direct: screen discomfort is commonly attributed to reduced blinking and prolonged near focus, and the AAO suggests the 20-20-20 rule (every 20 minutes look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds) and artificial tears for dryness.[6]

Tired-looking eyes, dark circles and a drained complexion are among the visible signs people associate with poor sleep. In experimental work from a Swedish group, sleep-restricted participants were photographed and rated by observers; the authors reported lower perceived health and attractiveness after restricted sleep, and a later study measured skin tone, eye opening, mouth shape and darkness around the eyes.[5] Blue-light glasses are one of several evening tools (alongside phone night modes and consistent bedtimes) that people use in the hope of protecting sleep and so the rested look.[14] The link between the glasses themselves and facial appearance has not been tested directly.

Wikipedia's article on computer vision syndrome reports that a 2021 review found little support for blue-blocking glasses for digital eye strain, that double-blind trials did not show benefit from blue-filter lenses, and notes an earlier amber-lens study that a follow-up did not reproduce, plus a lens-industry-sponsored study in which most participants could not detect changes.[1] The AAO says there is no scientific evidence that blue light from screens damages the eyes, attributes eye strain mainly to reduced blinking, and does not recommend blue-blocking glasses for computer use.[6] The UK College of Optometrists, as quoted on Wikipedia, states that the best available evidence does not support blue-blocking spectacle lenses for visual performance, eye fatigue, sleep or macular health.[4]
Grokipedia describes the picture as mixed, citing a questionnaire study suggesting benefit and a limited short-term effect, though its account contains internal inconsistencies.[2]

A pilot crossover study of 15 recreational athletes compared amber-lens glasses with clear glasses over four nights each and reported a shorter subjective sleep onset latency (about 7 minutes) with light restriction.[7] A double-blind randomized trial in 60 pregnant women compared full blue-blocking glasses with partial blockers for two weeks, and the primary sleep measures (total sleep time, midpoint of sleep) showed no significant group differences.[8] A companion report from the same trial examined melatonin profiles.[15] A single-blinded randomized trial in Norway added blue-blocking glasses from 6 p.m. to 8 a.m. for seven days to treatment as usual in hospitalised patients with bipolar mania, and reported a larger fall in Young Mania Rating Scale scores in the glasses group than the clear-lens group.[9]

Randomized trials include the athlete crossover pilot (n=15), the pregnancy trial (n=60), and the mania trial (12 glasses, 11 placebo patients analysed), described above.[7][8][9] Studies of glasses that emit blue light include a 2022 study in 15 patients with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder given roughly 470 nm morning light, a 2019 patient-experience survey in Parkinson disease, and a 2026 randomized pilot in 30 people with Parkinson disease (blue versus red light glasses for one hour twice daily over two weeks) that reported better Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores with blue light.[10][11][12] A 2023 cross-sectional survey of students at one university examined the prevalence of computer vision syndrome after the shift to online learning.[16] No studies were found testing blue-light glasses for making the eyes look brighter or less red.

Grokipedia reports that clinical reviews describe minimal risks for these lenses, that claims of dependency on the glasses lack supporting evidence, and that tinted lenses can alter colour perception.[2] Strongly tinted amber lenses change how colours look, which matters for tasks such as colour-critical work or driving at night.

On T Nation, glasses come up as one item in sleep-hygiene advice, for example a post recommending a blue light filter on devices and glasses alongside dietary changes to help dreams and nervous system calm.[14] Another poster suggests blue-light glasses and unplugging electronics among steps to support natural hormone levels after stopping TRT.[17] A 2020 Hacker News link carried a headline claiming research found that blue-light glasses improve sleep and workday productivity.[18] Discussion generally places the glasses within a bundle of sleep habits and not as a stand-alone fix.

Products range from clear coated lenses that filter a small share of blue light to amber and orange lenses that filter much more and visibly change colour. Independent spectrophotometry has shown that consumer products differ in how much blue light they transmit.[3] Prescription lenses can include blue-filter coatings, and the AAO notes that glasses prescribed for typical screen distance are a different product from blue-blockers.[6][4]

lore.intro: In fitness and recovery forums, blue-light glasses are one of several sleep-hygiene tools mentioned in passing, usually next to phone filters and consistent bedtimes.[14]
